pedagogy.summary: At upper KS2 the immune system is taught as the body's DEFENCE against germs (bacteria and viruses), in layers. First, barriers: the skin is the body's wall keeping germs out (and other barriers like mucus). If germs get in, WHITE BLOOD CELLS — defenders that patrol the blood — identify and destroy them. Finally, VACCINES: they contain weakened or inactive germs (or germ pieces) that safely TRAIN the immune system to recognise a specific disease, so if the real one ever appears the body already knows how to beat it. The organising idea is 'layers of defence' plus the powerful notion that the body can LEARN and remember an enemy — which is why a vaccine given now protects later. Ground it in the child's experience (a scab sealing a cut, why we get vaccinations) and connect to the cells–tissues–organs hierarchy (white blood cells are cells with a defence job). Keep specifics qualitative — named cell types, antibodies and the innate/adaptive split belong to the KS3 topic; the misconception to fix is that medicines/antibiotics are the same as the body's own immune defence.
bestPractices: Teach defence as LAYERS: barrier (skin) first, then white blood cells inside — so children see a system, not a single mechanism.
Frame white blood cells as the body's own defenders that find and destroy germs, linking to the cells–tissues–organs idea (they are cells with a job).
Explain vaccines as TRAINING/practice, not a cure: a safe rehearsal with a harmless version so the body is ready for the real disease — the key, counter-intuitive idea.
Anchor in experience: a scab sealing a cut (barrier repair), feeling unwell as the body fights infection, and why we get jabs — so defence is concrete.
Keep it qualitative and correct the 'medicine does the fighting' idea — the body's own immune system does the defending; distinguish it from antibiotics/painkillers.
keyRepresentations: Layered-defence diagram: skin barrier outside, white blood cells patrolling inside
White blood cell 'defender' finding and engulfing/destroying a germ
Vaccine-as-training: a harmless practice germ so the body learns to recognise the real one
A scab/cut-healing image for the barrier and its repair
Germ types (bacteria vs virus) as the invaders being defended against
commonMisconceptions: 'Medicine/antibiotics do the fighting' — rather than the body's OWN immune system doing the defending.
'Vaccines give you the disease' — they use weakened/inactive germs or pieces to train the body safely.
'Vaccines cure a disease you already have' — they prevent by training in advance, not treat after.
'Germs are all the same' — missing that bacteria and viruses are different kinds of invader.
'The skin is just a covering' — missing its role as the first line of defence (a barrier).
'Once germs are in, nothing can stop them' — missing the active role of white blood cells.
'Being unwell means the body is losing' — symptoms often show the immune system actively fighting.

learn.summary: Teach the immune system (ages 9–11) as the body's layered DEFENCE against germs (bacteria and viruses): first the skin as a barrier keeping germs out, then white blood cells that patrol inside and find and destroy germs that get in, and finally vaccines that safely TRAIN the body in advance to recognise a specific disease. The organising ideas are 'layers of defence' and that the body can learn and remember an enemy, which is why a vaccine given now protects later. Anchor in experience (a scab sealing a cut, feeling unwell while fighting infection, why we get jabs) and connect white blood cells to the cells–tissues–organs hierarchy (cells with a defence job). Keep it qualitative; named cell types, antibodies, and the innate/adaptive split belong to later study. The central misconception to fix is that medicines/antibiotics are the same as the body's own immune defence, and the counter-intuitive idea to land is that a vaccine trains rather than cures or infects.

activities.title: Defend the body: barrier, defenders, and the vaccine comparison
feedback: If a learner says the vaccine itself kills the germs, point them back to the two runs: the white blood cells do the destroying in both; the vaccine only changes how quickly they recognise the germ.

If a learner thinks the practice germ made the body ill, highlight that the harmless/weakened version is enough to be recognised but not to cause the disease — some people get a sore arm or feel a bit tired for a day or so while the body learns, but that is not the illness itself.
If a learner treats the skin as 'just a covering', replay germs being blocked at the barrier before any reach the blood.
Reinforce that seeing the SAME infection go two ways shows the only difference is prior training, not a cure applied after illness.
activities.rationale: A learner-driven dynamic model can let children see cause and effect in an active process — germs breaching a barrier, white blood cells hunting, and a vaccine changing the outcome. A before/after comparison of the same infection is intended to make the 'train first, win later' idea concrete, which is the counter-intuitive core of the topic. The toggle and two-run comparison are optional interaction examples offered to make the learning mechanism concrete, not mandatory mechanisms.
sourceClaims: Vaccines train the body's immune system by containing weakened or dead germs (or just surface proteins/sugars), triggering the same protective response as a real invader without causing illness, so the body can recognise and defeat the real disease later; vaccines prevent rather than treat disease.
The immune system defends the body in layers — physical barriers such as the skin, then white blood cells that identify and destroy bacteria and viruses that get inside.
learnerActions: Watch or help as germs swarm the skin barrier and a few slip through; follow the white blood cells patrolling the blood as they chase down and destroy the germs inside.
Run the infection first with NO vaccine: notice the body struggles and takes a long time to win.

Then give a vaccine first — a harmless 'practice' germ (or part of one) that the white blood cells learn to recognise — and run the SAME infection again; observe the defenders recognise the real germ much faster and defeat it, in this model before illness sets in (in real life a vaccine usually prevents the illness or makes it milder, but not always).
Compare the two runs side by side and state in your own words what the vaccine did (and did not do).
Open the myth-flap 'Does the jab make me sick?' and explain why the practice germ is safe.
activities.intendedInsight: Immune defence is an active process in layers: the skin is a barrier, white blood cells actively hunt and destroy germs inside, and a vaccine does not fight the disease for you or give it to you — it trains your own body in advance so the real germ is defeated faster.

activities.title: Reveal the layers of defence
feedback: If a learner merges the layers, ask which one keeps germs OUT and which one destroys germs that got IN.
On the vaccine flap, confirm that a weakened/inactive germ or a piece of it is enough to be recognised but not to cause disease.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal layered picture teaches the components and the vaccine idea clearly and supports learners who need the structure before the dynamics. Note its limit: a static reveal does not animate the hunt or the train-then-win comparison, so it works best as a scaffold alongside the dynamic activity.
sourceClaims: The immune system defends the body in layers — physical barriers such as the skin, then white blood cells that identify and destroy bacteria and viruses that get inside.
learnerActions: Tap or lift each layer in turn: the skin barrier outside, then the white blood cell defender patrolling inside, then the vaccine 'training card'.
Describe what each layer does in its own words before revealing the explanation.
Lift the flap on 'Does a vaccine give you the illness?' and say why the answer is no.
activities.intendedInsight: The body defends in distinct layers with different jobs — barrier (skin), active defence (white blood cells), and prevention by training in advance (vaccines).

activities.title: Consolidate: order, match, and judge
feedback: For 'a vaccine gives you the disease', clarify the germ in the vaccine is weakened/inactive or a fragment — enough to be recognised, not enough to cause illness.

For 'medicine does the fighting', shift agency back to the immune system: painkillers only ease how you feel and do not fight germs; antibiotics can help kill bacteria (not viruses), but your own white blood cells do the main recognising and destroying, and a vaccine trains them.
For 'antibiotics cure any germ', distinguish bacteria (antibiotics can treat) from viruses (they cannot), which is why prevention and the immune response matter.
For 'you catch a cold just from being cold', establish that infectious illness is caused by germs entering the body; being cold does not itself infect you.
For 'bacteria and viruses are the same', note they are different kinds of germ — one reason the same treatment does not work for both.
activities.rationale: Ordering, matching, and true/false items give a clean assessable consolidation of the components and myth-busting. Note the objective limit: recognition-style responses check recall and discrimination but do not elicit the learner's own constructed explanation of the training/memory mechanism — pair with the diagnostic prompt for that.
learnerActions: Sequence the layers of defence: barrier (skin) → white blood cells inside.
Match each component to its job (skin → keeps germs out; white blood cell → finds and destroys germs; vaccine → trains the body in advance).
Judge true/false statements that target vaccine and medicine misconceptions, e.g. 'A vaccine gives you the disease', 'Medicine, not your body, does the fighting' or 'Antibiotics cure any germ'.
Judge true/false statements about the cause and types of germs, e.g. 'You catch a cold just from being cold, not from germs' and 'Bacteria and viruses are exactly the same kind of germ'.
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can recall and distinguish the roles of barrier, defender cells, and vaccine, reject common vaccine myths, and recognise that infectious illness is caused by germs — with bacteria and viruses being different kinds of invader.

activities.title: Ask the doctor about vaccines (optional companion)
feedback: If the learner still expects to feel ill from the jab, reaffirm the weakened/inactive/fragment germ is recognised without causing the disease; a sore arm or feeling a bit tired for a day or so can happen, but that is the body learning, not the illness.
If asked about boosters, explain that the body's 'memory' of the practice germ can fade over time, so a booster re-trains the white blood cells to keep protection strong.
Steer explanations back to the body's own white blood cells doing the defending.
activities.rationale: A question-and-answer companion may address the vaccine misconceptions and the booster idea directly through factual dialogue. It is proposed as a secondary support to supplement explanation rather than carry the core concept; the active defence process may be more concretely conveyed through the dynamic model, but efficacy of either medium is untested here.
sourceClaims: Vaccines train the body's immune system by containing weakened or dead germs (or just surface proteins/sugars), triggering the same protective response as a real invader without causing illness, so the body can recognise and defeat the real disease later; vaccines prevent rather than treat disease.
learnerActions: Pose questions such as 'Why do I need a jab if I feel fine?' or 'Why doesn't the vaccine make me ill?'
Ask the follow-up 'Why might I need a booster later?' and restate what a booster does.
Read the factual reply and restate the 'train in advance' idea in your own words.
activities.intendedInsight: A vaccine is given when you are well because its job is to train your defences in advance, not to cure or to infect you; a booster is a reminder dose that re-trains the body if its 'memory' of the germ fades over time.

constraints: Keep specifics qualitative: named cell types, antibodies, and the innate/adaptive distinction belong to later study and should not be introduced here.

Immunity is enrichment at this stage; ground it in the child's experience (scab sealing a cut, feeling unwell while fighting, why we get jabs) and connect white blood cells to the cells–tissues–organs hierarchy.
The reveal/tap picture is a scaffold for the components and does not animate the hunt or the train-then-win comparison; use it alongside, not instead of, a dynamic comparison.
Recognition-style quiz items (sequence, match, true/false) do not elicit an independently constructed explanation of the training/memory mechanism; pair them with an open diagnostic prompt.
The 'ask the doctor' dialogue is an optional companion, not the primary means of teaching the active defence process; do not treat it as evidence that dialogue is superior or inferior to other media.
Distinguish the body's own immune defence from antibiotics/painkillers; do not let learners equate taking medicine with the immune system doing the fighting.
Establish germs (bacteria and viruses) as the cause of infectious illness, and that bacteria and viruses are different kinds of germ; being cold does not itself infect a person.
The before/after vaccine toggle and side-by-side runs are illustrative interaction examples, not required implementations.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit: the biological framing is consistent with the cited public-health/immunology sources (layered barrier → white blood cells → vaccine training; vaccines prevent rather than treat; weakened/inactive germ or fragment is recognised without causing disease). No arithmetic or force/motion claims were present to check.
One source (British Society for Immunology) is marked verified:false in the row; treat the layered-defence claim as reported rather than independently confirmed here.

The original row asserted that 3D 'adds no conceptual value' and that a process is 'better shown than told'; these are catalog fit judgements, not established comparative-efficacy claims, and have been removed or softened to narrowly scoped affordance/limit statements with proposed/may wording.

Restored coverage of two source-assessment misconceptions absent from the earlier candidate ('illness comes from cold weather, not germs' and 'bacteria and viruses are the same'), and restored the source's booster/waning-immunity extension in the optional companion.

Simplifications retained from the source (e.g. 'germs' covering bacteria and viruses, vaccine as 'training', immune 'memory') are age-appropriate but are models; they omit named cells and antibodies by design.

probeDeeper: If a vaccine trains your white blood cells, why might you need a 'booster' vaccine later on?
A friend says 'I never get vaccinated — I'm fine because medicine will cure me if I get sick.' What's risky about relying on that instead?
How is the skin's job in defending you different from the white blood cells' job?
assess.correctAnswer: The vaccine shows the immune system a harmless version (weakened, inactive, or just a piece) of the germ, so the white blood cells learn to recognise and 'remember' it — without the person getting ill, because the germ in the vaccine is too weak or inactive to cause disease. If the real, dangerous germ arrives later, the immune system already recognises it and destroys it fast, before it makes the person sick. The vaccine trains the body's own defences in advance.

errorPatterns.pattern: A vaccine gives you the disease, or a small case of it, so you get ill and then recover.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Clarify the germ in the vaccine is weakened/inactive/a fragment — enough to be recognised, not enough to cause disease.
errorPatterns.distractor: It works by giving you a small case of the disease so you get it and then it's over.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the vaccine infects you with the illness.

errorPatterns.pattern: Medicine or the vaccine kills the germs directly — your body doesn't do the fighting.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Shift agency to the immune system: the vaccine trains YOUR white blood cells; they do the recognising and destroying.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Attributes protection to the vaccine or medicine killing germs, not to training white blood cells.

errorPatterns.pattern: Antibiotics or medicine can cure any germ, including viruses like a cold.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Distinguish bacteria (antibiotics can treat) from viruses (they can't); this is why prevention and the immune response matter.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says antibiotics kill viruses / cure colds.

errorPatterns.pattern: You get ill from cold weather or being cold, not from germs.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Establish germs (bacteria/viruses) as the cause of infectious illness; cold weather doesn't itself infect you.
errorPatterns.distractor: You don't need germs — you get the illness just from being cold.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Names being cold, rather than germs, as the cause of illness.

responseLevels.gap: Thinks the vaccine gives you the disease, or that medicine/the vaccine kills germs directly with no role for the body's own defences.
responseLevels.full: Explains that the vaccine exposes the immune system to a harmless version so white blood cells learn and remember it, protecting against the real germ later, and distinguishes barriers (skin), active defence (white cells), and prevention (vaccines) — reasoning about boosters or non-vaccination.
responseLevels.partial: Knows white blood cells fight germs and vaccines help, but can't explain the training/memory mechanism — why a weakened germ protects without causing illness.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A vaccine is made from weakened or inactive germs, and you get it when you are NOT sick. How can putting a bit of a germ into a healthy person PROTECT them from that disease later? And why doesn't the vaccine give them the disease?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks the vaccine gives a mild case of the disease, or that medicine does the fighting instead of the body, reveals the gap. Only a child who grasps 'train and remember' explains protection without illness. The tier-two 'why doesn't it give the disease' forces the weakened/harmless-plus-memory idea.
